In [[mathematics]], the '''Kronheimer–Mrowka basic classes''' are elements of the second [[cohomology]] <math>H^2(M;\Z)</math> of a [[Simply connected space|simply connected]], smooth [[4-manifold]] <math>M</math> of simple type that determine its [[Donaldson theory|Donaldson polynomials]]. They were introduced by {{harvs|txt | last1=Kronheimer | first1=Peter B.| author1-link=Peter Kronheimer| last2=Mrowka | first2=Tomasz S. |author2-link=Tomasz Mrowka|  year1=1994 |year2=1995}}.

== Description ==
For a 4-manifold <math>M</math>, its [[Donaldson invariant|Donaldson invariants]] are an [[integer]] <math>\gamma_0(M)\in\mathbb{Z}</math> and maps <math>\gamma_d(M)\colon H_2(M,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}[1/2]</math> (into half-integers), which combine into the Donaldson polynomial:<ref>Kronheimer & Mrowka 1994, p. 3</ref><ref>Naber 11, p. 399</ref>

: <math>
\mathcal{D}_M\colon H_2(M,\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow\mathbb{R},
\mathcal{D}_M(x)
=\sum_{d=0}^\infty\frac{\gamma_d(M)(x)}{d!}.
</math>
Peter Kronheimer and Tomasz Mrowka introduced a condition known as Kronheimer–Mrowka simple type (KM simple type), which is sufficient to obtain the separate Donaldson invariants from their common Donaldson polynomial. For a KM-simple manifold <math>M</math> there are cohomology classes <math>K_1,\ldots,K_s\in H^2(M,\mathbb{Z})</math>, called Kronheimer–Mrowka basic classes (KM basic classes), as well as rational numbers <math>a_1,\ldots,a_s\in\mathbb{Q}</math>, called Kronheimer–Mrowka coefficients (KM coefficients), so that:

: <math>
\mathcal{D}_M(x)
=\exp(Q_M(x,x)/2)\sum_{r=1}^sa_r\exp(K_r(x))
</math>

for all <math>x\in H_2(M,\mathbb{Z})</math>. Furthermore <math>w_2(M)=K_r\operatorname{mod}2\in H^2(M,\mathbb{Z}_2)</math> for all Kronheimer–Mrowka basic classes.<ref>Kronheimer & Mrowka 94, Proposition 3</ref><ref>Kronheimer & Mrowka 95, Theorem 1.7</ref><ref>Naber 11, Theorem A.5.1</ref>

Although this reduction of the infinite sum of the Donaldson polynomial to a finite sum in early 1994 brought a significant simplification to Donaldson theory, it was overhauled just a few months later in late 1994 by the development of [[Seiberg–Witten theory]]. [[Edward Witten]], presented  in a lecture at [[MIT]], used a purely physical argument to conjecture that Kronheimer–Mrowka basic classes are exactly the [[Support (mathematics)|support]] of the [[Seiberg–Witten invariant]]s <math>\operatorname{SW}\colon
\operatorname{Spin}^\mathrm{c}(M)\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}</math> (hence the first [[Chern class]] <math>c_1\colon
\operatorname{Spin}^\mathrm{c}(M)\rightarrow H^2(M,\mathbb{Z})</math> of [[Spinc structure|spin<sup>c</sup> structures]] with a non-vanishing Seiberg–Witten invariant) and their Kronheimer–Mrowka coefficients are up to a topological factor exactly their Seiberg–Witten invariants. More concretely, it claims that a [[Compact space|compact]] [[Connected space|connected]] [[Simply connected space|simply connected]] orientable smooth 4-manifold <math>M</math> with <math>b_2^+(M)\geq 2</math> odd is of Kronheimer–Mrowka simple type if and only if is of Seiberg–Witten simple type (meaning non-vanishing Seiberg–Witten invariants only come from zero-dimensional [[Seiberg–Witten moduli space]]s by counting its points with a sign determined by their orientation). In this case the Donaldson polynomial is given by:<ref>Naber 11, p. 400</ref>

: <math>
\mathcal{D}_M(x)
=\exp(Q_M(x,x)/2)\sum_{\mathfrak{s}\in\operatorname{Spin}^\mathrm{c}(M), \dim\mathcal{M}_{\mathfrak{s}}^\mathrm{SW}=0}2^{2+\frac{1}{4}(7\chi(M)+11\sigma(M))}\operatorname{SW}(M,\mathfrak{s})\exp(c_1(\mathfrak{s})(x)).
</math>
